events.title: Indian National Congress founded
events.tooltip: Indian National Congress founded, 1885
events.summary: 72 delegates met at Bombay to launch the Indian National Congress, an early forum for educated Indian opinion within the imperial framework.
events.detail: The first session was convened by Allan Octavian Hume, a retired British civil servant, with W.C. Bonnerjee as president. Membership was overwhelmingly upper-caste, English-educated, and professional. The early Congress was avowedly loyalist — its demands were for greater Indian representation in the civil service and legislative councils, not independence. The radicalisation came later, accelerated by Curzon's partition of Bengal (1905) and the failure of moderate constitutionalism. By the 1920s the body that began as a debating society had become the political vehicle of a mass movement.

sources.label: Bipan Chandra et al., India's Struggle for Independence (1989)

events.title: Partition of Bengal
events.tooltip: Curzon partitions Bengal, 1905
events.summary: Curzon's split of Bengal into Hindu-majority west and Muslim-majority east galvanised the first mass agitation in colonial India.
events.detail: Lord Curzon argued the partition was an administrative measure for a province too large to govern. Indian opinion read it as a deliberate communal wedge. The Swadeshi movement that followed — boycott of British goods, promotion of Indian-made cloth, mass meetings in Calcutta — was the first agitation that successfully linked elite politics to street mobilisation. The partition was annulled in 1911 under King George V's Delhi Durbar, but the political memory remained. Bengal would be partitioned again in 1947, on lines roughly tracing Curzon's.

sources.label: Sumit Sarkar, Modern India 1885–1947 (1983)

events.title: Lajpat Rai writes The Story of My Deportation
events.tooltip: Lajpat Rai deported to Mandalay; writes account, 1907–1908
events.summary: Detained without trial under Regulation III, Lajpat Rai spent six months in Mandalay then published the first prison-writing of the Indian freedom movement.
events.detail: Lala Lajpat Rai was arrested in Lahore on 9 May 1907 under Regulation III of 1818 — the colonial law permitting indefinite detention without trial — for his agitation against the Punjab Colonization Bill and his role in the Swadeshi mobilisation. He was deported to Mandalay, Burma, and held in solitary confinement for six months before release on 11 November 1907 after a campaign by Indian nationalist opinion and Liberal MPs in the British Parliament. On return he wrote The Story of My Deportation, published Lahore 1908 — a 200-page first-person account of the arrest, the sea voyage, the Mandalay confinement, and the political reading he had carried with him. It is the earliest published prison-writing of the Indian freedom movement; the genre that would carry through Aurobindo, Gandhi at Yerwada, Bhagat Singh's notebooks, and Nehru's Discovery of India begins here.

caused_by.gloss: The Swadeshi mobilisation triggered by Curzon's Bengal partition spread to Punjab via Lajpat Rai's anti-Colonization-Bill agitation; the deportation was the colonial state's preferred response.

sources.label: Lala Lajpat Rai, The Story of My Deportation (Lahore: Punjabee Press, 1908)
V.C. Joshi (ed.), Lala Lajpat Rai: Writings and Speeches (2 vols., 1966)
Vijay Chandra Joshi, Lajpat Rai: Life and Work (1973)

events.title: Champaran Satyagraha
events.tooltip: Gandhi's first Indian satyagraha — Champaran indigo planters, 1917
events.summary: Champaran tenant Raj Kumar Shukla brought Gandhi to Bihar to investigate the indigo planter system; the resulting satyagraha was Gandhi's first inside India.
events.detail: The Champaran indigo system — 'tinkathia' — required ryots to plant 3 of every 20 katthas of their holding with indigo for European planters at fixed below-market prices, with debt bondage common. Raj Kumar Shukla, a Champaran tenant who had attended the 1916 Lucknow Congress session, persuaded Gandhi to visit. Gandhi reached Champaran on 10 April 1917, was served with an order to leave the district, refused, and was arrested. The case was withdrawn under public pressure; Gandhi conducted a six-month inquiry collecting testimony from approximately 8,000 ryots. The Champaran Agrarian Committee Report (October 1917) recommended abolition of tinkathia and partial restitution of overcharged rents. The Champaran Agrarian Act (1918) implemented the reforms. Champaran is the satyagraha that established Gandhi as a national figure inside India — the prior reputation was South African; this was the first Indian application of the same method.

sources.label: Rajendra Prasad, Champaran (1928, autobiographical account in Gujarati; Eng. trans. 1949)
Jacques Pouchepadass, Champaran and Gandhi: Planters, Peasants and Gandhian Politics (1999)

events.title: Jallianwala Bagh massacre
events.tooltip: Jallianwala Bagh massacre, Amritsar, 1919
events.summary: British troops under Brigadier-General Dyer fired without warning into a crowd of 15–20,000 gathered at an enclosed garden in Amritsar on Baisakhi.
events.detail: The Defence of India Act gave Punjab's Lt. Governor O'Dwyer wide powers, including bans on public assembly. Brigadier-General Reginald Dyer reached Amritsar on 11 April 1919. Two days later, on the festival of Baisakhi, a crowd had gathered in Jallianwala Bagh — an enclosed garden with a single narrow exit. Dyer marched in 50 riflemen, blocked the exit, and ordered fire without warning. Shooting continued for about ten minutes until ammunition was exhausted. Official British figures recorded 379 dead; the Congress inquiry put the toll above 1,000. The Hunter Commission later condemned Dyer's conduct, but Parliament voted him a public pension. The massacre converted constitutional moderates into nationalists nearly overnight.

sources.label: Kim A. Wagner, Jallianwala Bagh: An Empire of Fear and the Making of the Amritsar Massacre (2019)

events.title: Non-Cooperation Movement
events.tooltip: Non-Cooperation Movement, 1920–22
events.summary: Gandhi's first nationwide campaign — a boycott of British titles, courts, schools, and goods, joined to the Khilafat movement.
events.detail: Launched at the Calcutta Special Session of Congress in September 1920 and ratified at Nagpur in December, the Non-Cooperation Movement called for the surrender of British honours, withdrawal from government schools and courts, and a boycott of foreign cloth. By late 1921 it had reached scales no earlier campaign had: tens of thousands of students out of school, a near-total boycott of legislative elections, the Khilafat alliance giving it Hindu–Muslim breadth. Then, in February 1922, news arrived from Chauri Chaura. Gandhi suspended the movement within five days, against the wishes of nearly every senior Congress leader. He was arrested in March and sentenced to six years.

caused_by.gloss: The massacre and the Hunter Commission whitewash converted Gandhi from a constitutional cooperator into the architect of mass non-cooperation. He returned his Kaiser-i-Hind medal in protest.

sources.label: Judith M. Brown, Gandhi's Rise to Power: Indian Politics 1915–1922 (1972)

events.title: Chauri Chaura incident
events.tooltip: Chauri Chaura incident, 1922
events.summary: A procession in eastern UP killed 22 police and burned their station. Gandhi suspended the entire Non-Cooperation Movement within five days.
events.detail: On 4 February 1922, in a small market town in eastern United Provinces, a Khilafat–Non-Cooperation procession passed the Chauri Chaura police station. Police taunted the marchers, then opened fire when they refused to disperse, killing three. The crowd surged back, set fire to the station, and killed 22 policemen — most cut down as they fled the burning building. Gandhi received the news at Bardoli, where he was about to launch a no-tax campaign. Within five days he had unilaterally suspended the Non-Cooperation Movement, citing the violation of non-violence. Most Congress leaders disagreed publicly. Subhas Bose later called the suspension a 'national calamity.' Gandhi spent the next six years out of mass politics.

sources.label: Shahid Amin, Event, Metaphor, Memory: Chauri Chaura 1922–1992 (1995)

events.title: Gandhi writes The Story of My Experiments with Truth
events.tooltip: Gandhi writes Atmakatha at Sabarmati and Yerwada, 1925–1929
events.summary: Begun at Sabarmati after Chauri Chaura, Gandhi's Gujarati autobiography frames every choice — diet, household, satyagraha — as a moral experiment.
events.detail: Gandhi began the Atmakatha (autobiography) in Gujarati on 29 November 1925, serialised week by week in his journal Navjivan, with Mahadev Desai's English translation appearing simultaneously in Young India. Published in book form as Satyana Prayogo athva Atmakatha — Volume I in 1927, Volume II in 1929. Covers childhood at Porbandar, the years in England studying law, two decades in South Africa, return to India in 1915, and the satyagraha campaigns up to 1921 — deliberately stopping before the Chauri Chaura suspension. The 'experiments' framing is the book's signature move: every decision (vegetarianism, brahmacharya, the spinning wheel, household money) is offered as a test in moral physics. Reads less as memoir than as Augustinian self-examination transposed to a colonial-era reformer. Among the most translated Indian books of the 20th century.

caused_by.gloss: The post-Chauri-Chaura pause in mass action freed Gandhi for the long autobiographical work that he had previously deferred; the book starts in 1925 because the movement isn't running.

links.label: Wikipedia: The Story of My Experiments with Truth

sources.label: M.K. Gandhi, An Autobiography or The Story of My Experiments with Truth (trans. Mahadev Desai; Navajivan, 1927–1929)
Ramachandra Guha, Gandhi Before India (2013) and Gandhi: The Years That Changed the World (2018)
Tridip Suhrud, 'Gandhi's Key Writings: In Search of Unity', in The Cambridge Companion to Gandhi (2011)

events.title: Selected Letters of Sarojini Naidu
events.tooltip: Sarojini Naidu's letters, Congress presidency to UP governorship, 1925–1947
events.summary: Letters from Sarojini Naidu's Congress presidency (1925) through her UP governorship (1947) — the woman in the inner circle of Indian leadership.
events.detail: Sarojini Naidu's collected correspondence — published in volumes from 1925 onward, expanded posthumously by her daughter Padmaja Naidu — is the most complete record of a woman in the inner circle of Indian political leadership across two decades. Letters to Gandhi (whom she nicknamed 'Mickey Mouse'), Nehru, Tagore, Edmund Gosse (her early literary mentor at Cambridge), Edwin Lutyens, Sir Akbar Hydari, and her own family at Hyderabad. Covers her Congress presidency (Kanpur 1925, the first Indian woman to hold the post), her command of the salt campaigns at Dharasana when Gandhi was arrested, the 1931 Round Table negotiations in London, the Quit India arrest and Aga Khan Palace detention, and her post-Independence governorship of the United Provinces (1947–49). Distinct from her better-known poetry — the letters reveal the political negotiator, the satyagraha logistician, the salon hostess of nationalist Hyderabad.

location.name: Hyderabad (home base; campaigns spanned the subcontinent)

sources.label: Makarand Paranjape (ed.), Sarojini Naidu: Selected Letters, 1890s to 1940s (Kali for Women, 1996)
Padmini Sengupta, Sarojini Naidu: A Biography (1966)
Tara Ali Baig, Sarojini Naidu: Portrait of a Patriot (1974)

events.title: Simon Commission protest, Lahore
events.tooltip: Simon Commission protest at Lahore, 1928
events.summary: An all-white commission on Indian constitutional reform was met with 'Simon Go Back' protests; Lala Lajpat Rai died of injuries from the Lahore demonstration.
events.detail: The Simon Commission, appointed in November 1927, contained no Indian members. Congress and the Muslim League both boycotted it. When the Commission reached Lahore on 30 October 1928, Lala Lajpat Rai led a demonstration that was charged by police; Rai was severely beaten and died on 17 November of injuries his physicians attributed to the assault. His death radicalised the next generation, including Bhagat Singh, who avenged him by shooting the British police officer J.P. Saunders in December 1928. The Commission's report, when finally published in 1930, was overtaken by events.

sources.label: Bipan Chandra et al., India's Struggle for Independence (1989), ch. 21

events.title: Lahore Session — Purna Swaraj declaration
events.tooltip: Lahore Session: Purna Swaraj, 1929
events.summary: The Lahore Congress declared 'complete independence' (Purna Swaraj) as its goal and authorised civil disobedience.
events.detail: Until 1929 Congress's official aim was Dominion status within the British Empire. The Lahore Session, with Jawaharlal Nehru as president, broke with that. The Purna Swaraj resolution committed Congress to complete independence and authorised the working committee to launch civil disobedience. At the stroke of midnight on 31 December 1929, on the banks of the Ravi, the tricolour was unfurled. 26 January 1930 was declared the first Independence Day; the date was kept as Republic Day after 1950. The session also gave Gandhi the authority that he would exercise three months later at Dandi.

caused_by.gloss: The Simon boycott and Lajpat Rai's death persuaded Congress that the constitutional path was closed; Nehru and Bose pushed the dominion-status majority into the Purna Swaraj position.

sources.label: Sumit Sarkar, Modern India 1885–1947 (1983), ch. 6

events.title: Salt March (Dandi March)
events.tooltip: Salt March to Dandi, 1930
events.summary: Gandhi's 24-day march from Sabarmati Ashram to Dandi to break the British salt monopoly — the opening act of the Civil Disobedience Movement.
events.detail: On 12 March 1930 Gandhi and 78 hand-picked satyagrahis left Sabarmati Ashram for the coastal village of Dandi, 240 miles south. The march was deliberately slow — about 12 miles a day — to maximise press coverage and to recruit walkers from villages along the route. By the time they reached Dandi on 5 April, Gandhi led several thousand. On the morning of 6 April he stooped and picked up a lump of natural salt, breaking a tax law punishable by jail. The act triggered nationwide salt-making, mass arrests of perhaps 60,000 people, and the wider Civil Disobedience Movement. The discipline and theatre of the march — meticulous, slow, photographed daily — were Gandhi's answer to the chaos of Chauri Chaura eight years earlier.

caused_by.gloss: The Purna Swaraj resolution authorised civil disobedience and handed Gandhi the timing of its launch. He spent the next ten weeks selecting the salt tax as the symbolic target.

sources.label: Thomas Weber, On the Salt March: The Historiography of Gandhi's March to Dandi (1997)

events.title: Civil Disobedience Movement
events.tooltip: Civil Disobedience Movement, 1930–34
events.summary: Mass picketing of liquor and foreign-cloth shops, no-tax campaigns, and salt rush. Paused by the Gandhi–Irwin Pact, exhausted by 1934.
events.detail: The Salt March opened a wave of disobedience that took different shapes in different regions: mass picketing of liquor shops in Bombay and Madras, no-tax campaigns in Gujarat (Bardoli, Kheda) and the United Provinces, the Pathan Khudai Khidmatgars in the North-West Frontier, the salt rush on the Bengal and Madras coasts. The Gandhi–Irwin Pact of 5 March 1931 paused the movement; the Second Round Table Conference in London failed; the movement was revived in January 1932 and then ground down by mass arrests. Its political achievement was forcing Britain to legislate provincial autonomy in the Government of India Act 1935 — which fell well short of dominion status, but committed Whitehall to constitutional incrementalism it could not retreat from.

caused_by.gloss: The Salt March was both the opening act of the movement and its template — one symbolic, photographed act of law-breaking, replicated by millions.

sources.label: Bipan Chandra et al., India's Struggle for Independence (1989), ch. 23–24

events.title: Round Table Conferences
events.tooltip: Three Round Table Conferences in London, 1930–1932; Gandhi attends the second
events.summary: Three London conferences on Indian constitutional reform — Congress boycotted the first; Gandhi attended the second alone; the third seeded the 1935 Act.
events.detail: The British government convened three Round Table Conferences at St James's Palace, London, between November 1930 and December 1932 — the principal pre-1935 negotiation forum on Indian constitutional reform. The first (12 November 1930 – 19 January 1931) was boycotted by the Congress, then in jail under the Civil Disobedience Movement; it produced the federal-structure-with-princely-states framework but no Congress assent. The second (7 September – 1 December 1931) was attended by Gandhi alone for the Congress, after the Gandhi-Irwin Pact (5 March 1931) had suspended civil disobedience. Gandhi's insistence that Congress alone represented all Indians collided with separate-electorates demands from B.R. Ambedkar (for the Depressed Classes), the Muslim League, the Sikhs, and other interests; the conference deadlocked. The third (17 November – 24 December 1932) was attended by neither Congress nor most major Indian parties; it produced the constitutional framework that became the Government of India Act 1935 — the legal template the independent Indian Republic largely inherited in 1950.

sources.label: Sumit Sarkar, Modern India 1885–1947 (1983), ch. 6
Judith M. Brown, Gandhi: Prisoner of Hope (1989), ch. 7

events.title: Execution of Bhagat Singh, Rajguru, and Sukhdev
events.tooltip: Bhagat Singh, Rajguru, Sukhdev hanged at Lahore Central Jail, 23 March 1931
events.summary: Bhagat Singh, Shivaram Rajguru, Sukhdev Thapar hanged at Lahore Central Jail under the Lahore Conspiracy Case verdict — eleven hours before announced time.
events.detail: Bhagat Singh (23), Shivaram Rajguru (22), and Sukhdev Thapar (23), Hindustan Socialist Republican Association (HSRA) revolutionaries, were hanged at Lahore Central Jail on 23 March 1931 — eleven hours before the announced 6:00 AM execution time, to forestall public protests outside the jail. They had been convicted in the Lahore Conspiracy Case for the December 1928 killing of John Saunders, a Lahore police assistant superintendent (mistaken for the senior officer responsible for the lathi-charge that killed Lala Lajpat Rai weeks earlier), and for the April 1929 Bhagat-Singh-and-Batukeshwar-Dutt bombing of the Central Legislative Assembly in Delhi (a deliberately non-lethal protest, leaflets reading 'it takes a loud noise to make the deaf hear'). The trial — held in absentia for portions when the defendants refused to participate — became a major political event; Gandhi failed to secure clemency in his Round Table negotiation with Lord Irwin. The bodies were cremated secretly at Hussainiwala on the Sutlej; Bhagat Singh has the distinction of being among the most-cited Indian revolutionaries across ideologically opposed political traditions in the post-1947 period.

caused_by.gloss: The Simon protest produced the lathi-charge that killed Lajpat Rai; the HSRA's revenge-killing of Saunders in December 1928 was the proximate act for which Bhagat Singh and Rajguru were tried, alongside the Assembly bombing.

sources.label: A.G. Noorani, The Trial of Bhagat Singh: Politics of Justice (1996; rev. 2005)
Chaman Lal (ed.), Bhagat Singh: The Jail Notebook and Other Writings (2007)

events.title: Poona Pact between Gandhi and Ambedkar
events.tooltip: Gandhi-Ambedkar Poona Pact, 24 September 1932; ends Gandhi's Yerwada fast
events.summary: Gandhi's six-day Yerwada fast against the Communal Award ended with the Poona Pact — reserved seats in joint electorate replacing separate electorates.
events.detail: The British Communal Award (16 August 1932), announced by Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald after the Round Table Conferences' deadlock, granted separate electorates to the Depressed Classes (Dalits) — separate from the Hindu electorate, with reserved constituencies in which only Dalits could vote. B.R. Ambedkar had argued for this as essential to political representation independent of the caste-Hindu elite. Gandhi, opposed on the principle that separate electorates would permanently divide the Hindu community, began a fast unto death at Yerwada Jail (Pune) on 20 September 1932. After six days of negotiation between Ambedkar and Hindu reformist intermediaries (Madan Mohan Malaviya, M.C. Rajah), the Poona Pact was signed on 24 September 1932: separate electorates were dropped in favour of joint electorates with substantially expanded reserved seats (148 for Depressed Classes in the provincial legislatures, against the Communal Award's 71). Ambedkar's later writings (notably What Congress and Gandhi Have Done to the Untouchables, 1945) read the Pact as a coerced settlement under fast pressure; the seat-reservation framework persists in the Indian constitution.

caused_by.gloss: The Round Table deadlock over separate electorates pushed MacDonald to impose the Communal Award unilaterally; Gandhi's fast and the resulting Poona Pact are the immediate political response to the Award.

sources.label: B.R. Ambedkar, What Congress and Gandhi Have Done to the Untouchables (Thacker, 1945)
Eleanor Zelliot, From Untouchable to Dalit (1992), ch. 5
Christophe Jaffrelot, Dr Ambedkar and Untouchability (2005), ch. 3

events.title: Ambedkar publishes Annihilation of Caste
events.tooltip: Ambedkar self-publishes Annihilation of Caste, Bombay, 1936
events.summary: Withdrawn from a Lahore reform conference for being too radical, Ambedkar self-published the address as a 96-page polemic and answered Gandhi's review.
events.detail: Ambedkar drafted Annihilation of Caste in 1935–36 as the presidential address for the Jat-Pat-Todak Mandal's annual conference at Lahore, scheduled May 1936. The Mandal — a Hindu reform body — read the text and withdrew the invitation when Ambedkar refused to alter the passages arguing that caste could not be reformed within Hinduism and that Hindus seeking equality should leave the religion. Ambedkar self-published the undelivered address as a 96-page book in May 1936 from Bombay. Gandhi published a hostile review in Harijan; Ambedkar replied with the polemical preface to the second edition (1937), which is now read as integral to the work. Among the most directly argued first-person texts in the Indian canon — not memoir as such but argued autobiography of an intellectual position, with the author's own life-story embedded as evidence in the polemic. The book reframed the caste question for the 20th century.

date.display: May 1936 (1st ed.); 1937 (2nd ed. with preface to Gandhi)

sources.label: B.R. Ambedkar, Annihilation of Caste (1936; annotated critical ed. S. Anand with introduction by Arundhati Roy, Navayana, 2014)
Christophe Jaffrelot, Dr Ambedkar and Untouchability: Analysing and Fighting Caste (2005)
Gail Omvedt, Ambedkar: Towards an Enlightened India (2004)

events.title: Subhas Chandra Bose writes The Indian Struggle
events.tooltip: Bose writes Indian Struggle in Vienna exile, 1934; pub. London 1935
events.summary: Deported from India after the 1932 arrests, Bose wrote a 400-page history of 1920–1934 in Vienna. Banned in India by the Raj on publication.
events.detail: Subhas Chandra Bose was deported to Europe in February 1933 after his second imprisonment under the Defence of India Rules. Through 1934, working from Vienna with secretarial help from Emilie Schenkl, he wrote The Indian Struggle 1920–1934 — a 400-page history of the Non-Cooperation, Civil Disobedience, and Round Table phases from a Bengal-Forward-Bloc vantage that was systematically critical of Gandhi's tactical choices. Published by Wishart in London, January 1935; banned in British India on publication. The completing volume covering 1935–1942 was written between his 1941 escape from Calcutta house arrest and his death in 1945; published posthumously 1948. Together the two volumes are the fullest first-person record of the Congress left's reading of the freedom struggle, distinct from both the Gandhian and the Nehruvian accounts.

date.display: Written Vienna 1934; pub. London Jan 1935 (vol. 2 posthumous 1948)

location.name: Calcutta (Bose's political base; written in Vienna exile)

sources.label: Subhas Chandra Bose, The Indian Struggle 1920–1942 (combined ed., Asia Publishing House, 1964)
Sugata Bose, His Majesty's Opponent: Subhas Chandra Bose and India's Struggle Against Empire (2011), ch. 6
Leonard A. Gordon, Brothers Against the Raj: A Biography of Indian Nationalists Sarat and Subhas Chandra Bose (1990)

events.title: Quit India Movement
events.tooltip: Quit India launched at Bombay, 1942
events.summary: Gandhi's 'Do or die' demand for immediate British withdrawal. With its leadership arrested, the movement spiralled into the largest uprising of the struggle.
events.detail: On 8 August 1942, the All-India Congress Committee meeting at Bombay's Gowalia Tank Maidan passed the Quit India resolution. Gandhi gave the speech containing the line 'Do or die' and was arrested before dawn on 9 August along with the entire Congress working committee. With its leadership in jail, the movement spiralled out of central control. Crowds attacked railway stations, post offices, and police outposts across Bihar, the United Provinces, and Bengal. British retaliation included machine-gun fire from low-flying aircraft. By the year's end, over 60,000 had been arrested and roughly 1,000 killed. Quit India is often called the last mass movement of the freedom struggle — by the time the Congress leaders were released in 1945, the political question was no longer whether Britain would leave, only when and on what terms.

sources.label: Sumit Sarkar, Modern India 1885–1947 (1983), ch. 7
Bipan Chandra et al., India's Struggle for Independence (1989), ch. 32

events.title: Nehru writes The Discovery of India
events.tooltip: Nehru drafts Discovery of India, Ahmednagar Fort, 1944–45
events.summary: Imprisoned after Quit India, Nehru wrote The Discovery of India between April 1944 and September 1945 — the third book of his prison trilogy, published 1946.
events.detail: Arrested on 9 August 1942 and held without trial, Nehru spent 1,041 days in Ahmednagar Fort with eleven other Congress leaders. Between April 1944 and September 1945 he drafted the 600-page Discovery of India in longhand, working through readings supplied by Maulana Azad and Pattabhi Sitaramayya among others. The book argues for an Indian civilisational continuity — Vedic, Buddhist, Mughal, modern — that could underwrite a secular republic, against both colonial 'no India before us' historiography and Hindu-nationalist communal essentialism. It was published in 1946 by Signet Press, Calcutta, completing his prison trilogy after Glimpses of World History (1934) and Toward Freedom (1936). The framing — composite, civilisational, secular — would become the founding ideology of the Indian state Nehru led from 1947.

caused_by.gloss: The Quit India arrests put Nehru and the entire Congress working committee in Ahmednagar Fort for nearly three years; Discovery of India is the most ambitious of the books that came out of that confinement.

sources.label: Jawaharlal Nehru, The Discovery of India (Signet Press, 1946)
Sarvepalli Gopal, Jawaharlal Nehru: A Biography, Vol. 1 (1975), ch. 18
Benjamin Zachariah, Nehru (Routledge, 2004), ch. 4

events.title: INA at Imphal–Kohima
events.tooltip: Battle of Imphal–Kohima, March–July 1944; Bose's INA + Japanese 15th Army
events.summary: Subhas Bose's Azad Hind Fauj fought with the Japanese 15th Army at Imphal–Kohima, March–July 1944 — the high water of the Burma campaign before defeat.
events.detail: Subhas Chandra Bose, having escaped Calcutta house arrest in January 1941 and reached Berlin then (via U-boat) Tokyo in 1943, took command of the Indian National Army (Azad Hind Fauj — INA) on 4 July 1943 and proclaimed the Provisional Government of Azad Hind at Singapore on 21 October 1943. The INA, fighting alongside the Imperial Japanese Army's 15th Army under Lt-Gen Renya Mutaguchi, launched the U-Go operation in March 1944 — crossing the Chindwin and pushing into Manipur and the Naga Hills. The Battles of Imphal (8 March – 3 July 1944) and Kohima (4 April – 22 June 1944) were the campaign's twin peaks: Kohima's Tennis Court battle is among the most-cited British-Indian military engagements of WWII. The British 14th Army under General William Slim broke the Japanese-INA advance through superior logistics and air supply; an estimated 53,000 Japanese-INA casualties (mostly to disease and starvation in monsoon retreat) versus 16,500 Allied. The defeat ended Japanese hopes in the Burma theatre and the INA's military project; the 1945–46 INA trials at the Red Fort in Delhi (Shah Nawaz Khan, P.K. Sahgal, G.S. Dhillon) became a major nationalist political event in the run-up to independence.

caused_by.gloss: Bose's exile-political project documented in The Indian Struggle and continued at Berlin/Tokyo culminated in the INA campaign — Imphal–Kohima is the military extension of the political work the 1935 book frames.

sources.label: Sugata Bose, His Majesty's Opponent: Subhas Chandra Bose and India's Struggle Against Empire (2011)
Robert Lyman, Slim, Master of War (2004)
Joyce Lebra, The Indian National Army and Japan (1971; rev. 2008)

events.title: Direct Action Day, Calcutta
events.tooltip: Direct Action Day, Calcutta, 1946
events.summary: The Muslim League's call for 'direct action' triggered four days of communal killings in Calcutta. Roughly 4,000 dead. The case for a united India was broken.
events.detail: After the failure of the Cabinet Mission Plan to keep India united, the Muslim League called for Direct Action Day on 16 August 1946. In Calcutta, the only major city with a League-led provincial government, the demonstration tipped into four days of communal violence — initiated by League cadres, met and exceeded by Hindu and Sikh crowds. Estimates put the dead between 4,000 and 10,000, with some 100,000 wounded or homeless. The 'Great Calcutta Killings' destroyed whatever residual belief existed in the political class that an undivided India could be governed; from there, partition was a question of when and how, not whether. The violence spread to Bihar (October), Noakhali (October–November), and the Punjab (March 1947) before culminating in the partition migrations.

sources.label: Yasmin Khan, The Great Partition: The Making of India and Pakistan (2007)

events.title: Independence and Partition
events.tooltip: Independence and Partition, 1947
events.summary: India and Pakistan became independent on 14–15 August 1947. The migrations and killings that followed were the largest population transfer in human history.
events.detail: India became independent at midnight on 14–15 August 1947; Pakistan a day earlier. The line dividing them — drawn by Cyril Radcliffe, who had never visited India — was published only on 17 August. The intervening uncertainty cost lives. An estimated 14 million people crossed in the largest migration in human history; between 200,000 and two million were killed in the violence that accompanied it, mostly in Punjab and Bengal. The structures of the new states were inherited largely intact — civil service, army, currency, parliamentary form — but the cost of the transfer of power was paid in the millions of lives uprooted along an arbitrary line. Nehru's 'tryst with destiny' speech to the Constituent Assembly, delivered hours before midnight, did not mention partition.

caused_by.gloss: Quit India settled the question of whether Britain would leave; what remained was when and on what terms.
The Calcutta killings destroyed the political consensus around a united India and made partition the path of least resistance for a departing power.

sources.label: Yasmin Khan, The Great Partition (2007)
Ramachandra Guha, India After Gandhi (2007), ch. 1–2

events.title: Maulana Azad dictates India Wins Freedom
events.tooltip: Azad's partition memoir, dictated Delhi 1957–58, suppressed pages opened 1988
events.summary: Azad dictated his partition memoir to Humayun Kabir 1957–58; the 30-page section critical of Nehru and Patel was sealed for 30 years.
events.detail: Maulana Abul Kalam Azad — Congress President 1939–46, India's first Education Minister, the senior Muslim Congress leader through partition — dictated his memoir India Wins Freedom to his secretary Humayun Kabir between 1957 and his death in February 1958. Published February 1959. Covers the 1937–47 decade in detail: the Cripps Mission (1942), Quit India and Azad's Ahmednagar Fort imprisonment with Nehru, the Cabinet Mission (1946), Mountbatten's June 1947 plan, Azad's opposition to partition. The book's most controversial section — 30 pages dealing critically with Nehru and Patel's roles in accepting partition — was withheld at Azad's instruction until 1988, thirty years after his death. When opened in 1988, the suppressed pages caused political controversy in India for their direct criticism of the Nehru-Patel partition decisions. The fullest first-person record of partition negotiations from a Congress Muslim's perspective, and a deliberate act of posthumous score-settling.

caused_by.gloss: Azad's memoir is the longest-form first-person reckoning with the partition decision; the suppressed pages indict the Nehru-Patel acquiescence in the Mountbatten plan.

sources.label: Maulana Abul Kalam Azad, India Wins Freedom (Orient Longmans, 1959; complete edition with the suppressed pages, 1988)
